title: Checkpointing & Persistence
objective: After this lesson you will be able to scope threads, persist checkpoints per step, resume interrupted runs exactly, replay traces for debugging, and bound checkpoint cost by scoping state.
why: Crashes, deploys, approvals, and lunch all interrupt runs. Without persistence, every interruption restarts blind — re-sending emails, re-charging cards, losing the thread. Checkpointing (state snapshots per step, keyed by thread) converts interruptions into pauses: resume re-enters exactly, replay reproduces bugs deterministically, and audit trails write themselves.

blocks.text: A **thread** (`thread_id`) scopes one conversation's state across calls, crashes, and days. Same thread + same graph = continuing conversation; new thread = fresh state. Thread IDs are your design surface: per-ticket threads isolate customers, per-user threads carry history, and ID choice determines what 'remember me' even means.

blocks.caption: Threads make interruptions into pauses — same ID, full memory

blocks.text: What gets saved, when, and how big

Checkpoints snapshot **state per step** (values + which node runs next + step number). Cost scales with state size × steps × threads — which is why Ch.2's minimal/bounded virtues are economic, not aesthetic. Scope ruthlessly: decisions and digests persist; raw bulk lives outside with references. Measure checkpoint bytes per thread in development; surprise sizes mean state-design debt.

blocks.caption: Save deep copies per step; resume reads the latest; history enables replay

blocks.text: Three operations on history: **resume** (continue from latest after interruption), **replay** (re-run from step N with same inputs — deterministic debugging), **time-travel/fork** (resume from an earlier checkpoint with edited state — 'what if the approval differed?'). Replay needs deterministic nodes (same state → same outputs); time-travel needs validated edits (Ch.6). Together they make agent bugs reproducible — the end of 'works on my run'.

blocks.title: Crash, then resume
blocks.note: Run it: expect resume at step 1 -> draft, category shipping, missing thread null, history intact true. Deep-copy-on-save is the line that prevents history corruption — verify it, don't trust it.

items: Threads scope conversations: ID design defines what remembering means
Checkpoints snapshot state per step; cost scales with state size — minimal/bounded state is economic
Resume continues, replay reproduces, time-travel forks — deterministic nodes + validated edits required
Deep-copy on save; measure bytes per thread in development

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice checkpointer and confirm all four outputs. (b) Extend it with a history(thread) accessor returning step numbers, and a fork(thread, fromStep, edits) that resumes from an earlier checkpoint with validated edits. (c) State the production saver swap (MemorySaver → durable) and what survives a process restart in each case.
hints: Four outputs: step-1/draft resume, shipping category, null missing thread, deep-copy proof true.
history: map checkpoints to steps. fork: slice history to fromStep, merge validated edits over that state, continue — document that edits need schema validation (Ch.3).
MemorySaver dies with the process (dev only); durable savers (Postgres-backed) survive restarts — same compile() API, different durability.
exercise.why: History access plus validated forking completes the persistence toolkit: resume (operations), replay (debugging), fork (what-if). The saver swap teaches the dev/prod boundary — same API, different survival.
exercise.code: // history/fork pattern: slice checkpoints, validate edits, resume forward.

quiz.q: Same thread ID across two days of follow-ups gives…
options: Continuing state: full memory of prior steps — thread IDs define remembered scope
quiz.explain: Threads scope memory across time and crashes. ID design (per-ticket vs per-user) is a product decision about what continuity means.

quiz.q: Checkpoints grow 2MB per thread. First response?
options: Scope state minimally (Ch.2 virtues) and measure per-thread bytes — cost scales with state size × steps × threads
quiz.explain: Checkpoint economics trace to state design: raw bulk referenced outside, digests inside, bounded always. Size surprises are state-design debt surfacing.

quiz.q: Why deep-copy state on checkpoint save?
options: Later mutations would otherwise rewrite history — replay and audit need immutable snapshots
quiz.explain: Shared references corrupt the past: resume/replay/audit read history expecting truth. Copy-on-save freezes each step faithfully.

summary: Threads scope, checkpoints snapshot (deep-copied), resume continues, replay reproduces, forks explore. Persistence converts interruptions to pauses — designed via minimal state, verified via resume proofs.
next: Memory survives crashes — now pause deliberately for humans: approval gates, edit-and-resume, and interrupt placement. Next: human-in-the-loop.
